current_meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a <radical>samurai</radical> wedges his armoured shoulders through the gate and roars over the party. Sprawled at his boots is last night's <radical>corpse / body</radical>, still face-down on the mossy steps, undisturbed. That roar shaking the great bell awake is voice.

At school, the gym teacher chalks one flat line onto the <radical>ground</radical>, then a second beside it — <radical>two</radical> lines laid like chopsticks for the new drill. Two coaches grip the yardstick between them, <radical>two hands</radical> holding it dead level, until it tips off the bench and down a gravel <radical>slide</radical>, gone before anyone can grab it. Where it lands, someone rakes <radical>three</radical> claw-mark slashes through the chalk. That rough sketch scratched into the floor is a shape.

Three droplets flick off the wet paintbrush and splash into the <radical>water</radical> below a hot spring. A crooked roof-beam <radical>chevron</radical> lands askew on top like a hairpin. Flat layers of <radical>steam</radical> lie on the water, and the last wisp hooks up and peels into the cold — vapor rising off the pool.

A hiker flicks a coin off the mountain trail. It's on the <radical>slide</radical>, gone before anyone can react. Right at the <radical>ground</radical>, a <radical>barb</radical> flicks up and hooks the coin's edge, yanking it back. Snatching a falling coin like that: pure genius.

A field of grain bows low along the riverbank, each stalk bent double under a head so heavy it can't stand straight. Wind pushes it down further and it still doesn't snap, just dips lower and lower. That endless stooped bow is <radical>barley</radical>.

At Koichi's konbini a customer draws a long blade to slice open a stubborn onigiri wrapper. It sweeps down and hooks sharp at the tip, but the plastic fights back and chips a nick right at the top edge. Everyone stares at the scratched blade: an actual <radical>sword</radical>, ruined on rice packaging.

On Sei's sports field, the archery club lines up their weapons, stacked curves of springy wood bent back on themselves, notched at both ends where the string bites in. A coach pulls one taut until it hums, holding a <radical>bow</radical> ready to fire.

On the mountain trail, the vending machine's fan kicks up a strand shed by a passing dog. It hangs in the wind: a flat line at the scalp, hooking into a curl, flicking to a sharp point. It lands stuck to a hiker's sweaty arm, twisting there. That stray curling wisp is <radical>fur</radical>.
